question: What is the main job of red blood cells (erythrocytes) in the body?

options.B: Clotting blood at sites of vessel injury

explanation: Red blood cells specialize in gas transport, moving oxygen from the lungs to body tissues and carrying carbon dioxide back. [learn more](BMP111_U5_T2#BMP111_U5_T2_h1)

question: Why do newborn babies usually have higher red blood cell counts than adult women?

options.A: Infants experience rapid dehydration immediately after birth
options.B: Fetal hemoglobin requires fewer cells to carry enough oxygen
options.C: Neonatal bone marrow makes cells much larger in size
options.D: Newborns have higher oxygen demands relative to their mass

explanation: Neonates require higher baseline cell counts to meet the high metabolic and oxygen demands of early postnatal life. [learn more](BMP111_U5_T2#BMP111_U5_T2_h1)

question: What shape does a normal, mature human red blood cell have?
explanation: The biconcave disc shape provides a large surface area for efficient gas exchange while allowing the cell to deform easily. [learn more](BMP111_U5_T2#BMP111_U5_T2_h2)

question: Why is it important for red blood cells not to have mitochondria?

options.A: To prevent the cell from consuming the oxygen it carries
options.B: To allow room for the nucleus to control cell division
options.C: To speed up anaerobic energy production inside tissues
options.D: To protect the cell membrane from oxidative damage

explanation: Without mitochondria, red blood cells rely on anaerobic pathways and do not use up any of the oxygen they transport to tissues. [learn more](BMP111_U5_T2#BMP111_U5_T2_h2)

question: How many oxygen molecules can a single hemoglobin molecule carry when it is fully loaded?
explanation: Each hemoglobin molecule contains four iron-bearing heme groups, allowing it to transport a maximum of four oxygen molecules. [learn more](BMP111_U5_T2#BMP111_U5_T2_h3)

question: What does hemoglobin do when blood flows through active, working muscles?

options.A: It absorbs excess carbon dioxide and turns into white blood cells
options.B: It permanently locks its structure to store extra iron locally
options.C: It converts all iron atoms into the ferric state for storage
options.D: It readily releases its bound oxygen molecules to the tissue

explanation: Active tissues have lower oxygen tension and higher waste, prompting hemoglobin to unload its oxygen cargo to sustain cellular respiration. [learn more](BMP111_U5_T2#BMP111_U5_T2_h3)

question: Which organ in the body is mainly responsible for producing erythropoietin?
explanation: Specialized cells in the kidneys monitor blood oxygen levels and secrete erythropoietin to stimulate red blood cell production when oxygen is low. [learn more](BMP111_U5_T2#BMP111_U5_T2_h4)

question: What is a reticulocyte?

options.A: A worn-out erythrocyte being broken down in the spleen
options.B: A specialized white blood cell that fights viral infections
options.C: An immature red blood cell recently released from the bone marrow
options.D: A stem cell that has not yet committed to any specific lineage

explanation: Reticulocytes are youthful red blood cells that have lost their nucleus but still contain residual RNA from hemoglobin synthesis. [learn more](BMP111_U5_T2#BMP111_U5_T2_h4)

question: What is the average lifespan of a normal red blood cell in circulation?
explanation: Lacking a nucleus and repair mechanisms, red blood cells circulate for about 120 days before macrophage destruction. [learn more](BMP111_U5_T2#BMP111_U5_T2_h5)

question: When old red blood cells are broken down, what happens to the salvaged iron?

options.A: It is permanently stored inside the white blood cells
options.B: It is transported back to the bone marrow to make new cells
options.C: It is excreted immediately through the kidneys in urine
options.D: It is converted into bilirubin and eliminated in the stool

explanation: The body carefully conserves iron, binding it to transferrin and returning it to the bone marrow for the production of new erythrocytes. [learn more](BMP111_U5_T2#BMP111_U5_T2_h5)

question: What is the medical term for a condition where the blood has a low oxygen-carrying capacity due to a lack of red cells?
explanation: Anemia is characterized by a deficit in healthy red blood cells or hemoglobin, leading to reduced tissue oxygenation and fatigue. [learn more](BMP111_U5_T2#BMP111_U5_T2_h6)

question: Which physical sign is a midwife most likely to check when screening a pregnant woman for anemia?

options.A: Pallor of the conjunctiva and nail beds
options.B: Yellow discoloration of the skin and sclera
options.C: Increased skin temperature and rapid sweating
options.D: Red swelling over the primary joints of the hands

explanation: Reduced hemoglobin levels often manifest as pale mucous membranes and nail beds, making them quick clinical indicators of anemia. [learn more](BMP111_U5_T2#BMP111_U5_T2_h6)
